title: Harvey Power Users: The Champions Network — Alex Bazin at Lewis Silkin
author: Harvey Team · Alex Bazin

dom.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s view that tool acquisition alone is insufficient and materially develops it with a concrete adoption model: convert successful experiments into shared workflows, use workflow-aware champions, and reinforce uptake through sustained peer communication.
qs: If someone has found an effective way to use the tool for a specific task, the goal is to make that the default approach for everyone doing that work.
For organizations looking to scale adoption, the challenge isn’t just creating more power users, but building the systems that help their impact compound.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that organisational value depends on converting individual experimentation into repeatable workflows backed by champions, peer demonstrations and sustained reinforcement. Its usage figures also distinguish broad monthly engagement from more frequent use, while not establishing measured quality, profitability or client outcomes.
qs: But they’re often doing so individually — which means the next step is turning that experimentation into more structured, group-level adoption to drive scale and return.
They’re supported by the right environment — clear use cases, shared workflows, and consistent reinforcement.

kp.k: Lewis Silkin reports broad but uneven Harvey adoption
kp.d: Alex Bazin reports that two-thirds of Lewis Silkin users engage with Harvey monthly, with about half of that group using it at least weekly. His stated objective for 2026 is to increase consistency among occasional and inactive users and make Harvey the standard workflow for suitable tasks such as employment-tribunal chronologies.
qs: Two-thirds of our users engage with Harvey monthly, and about half of those use it at least weekly.
My focus this year is driving more consistent usage from everyone else, both those who use it occasionally and those who may have forgotten it exists.
Ideally, when someone is, for example, building a chronology for an employment tribunal, using Harvey isn’t optional — it’s the standard way the work gets done.

kp.k: Discretion makes generative AI adoption unusually difficult
kp.d: Bazin argues that generative AI differs from mandatory enterprise systems because lawyers can continue using established working methods. Adoption therefore depends on an individual decision at the point of work, even where AI may improve effectiveness, profitability, or client service; these benefits are asserted rather than quantified here.
qs: AI is unusual in that it’s highly discretionary.
With generative AI, you can continue working exactly as you always have.
You may be more effective, more profitable, and deliver better client service by using it, but the decision to use it still sits with the individual, in the moment.

kp.k: Power users identify scalable, high-value legal use cases
kp.d: Bazin says Lewis Silkin uses power users’ experimentation to identify valuable applications and disseminate them across the firm. The intended progression is from individual experimentation to structured adoption at practice-group level, increasing scale and return.
qs: Power users help us identify high-value use cases, which we can then share more broadly across the firm.
But they’re often doing so individually — which means the next step is turning that experimentation into more structured, group-level adoption to drive scale and return.
Take the results of individual experimentation and turn them into shared best practices.

kp.k: Embedded champions support adoption within existing practice workflows
kp.d: Lewis Silkin has created a network of Harvey champions embedded in practice groups to support, guide, and encourage use. Many champions are knowledge lawyers, allowing AI guidance to be incorporated into their established responsibility for training and legal updates; Bazin says champions need workflow understanding rather than being the most technically advanced users.
qs: We’ve also built a network of Harvey champions, who are individuals embedded within practice groups who can support, guide, and encourage adoption.

Many are knowledge lawyers, so this extends naturally from the training and updates they already provide: here’s the latest case law, here’s what’s changed, and here’s how people are using Harvey in this group.
Champions don’t need to be the most advanced users themselves.
They need to understand where the technology fits within existing workflows and help others adopt it.

kp.k: Peer demonstrations communicate practical use across organisational levels
kp.d: The firm runs all-hands “spotlights” in which three or four employees from legal and non-legal roles demonstrate real uses of Harvey. Bazin argues that success stories presented by peers at different seniority levels are more persuasive than top-down instructions from a central team.
qs: Alongside that, we run what we call “spotlights,” which are all-hands sessions where three or four people share how they’re using Harvey.
These speakers come from across the firm and at every level — from junior marketing managers to IP disputes partners to data associates — all showing practical, real-world use cases.
When a trainee and a partner can both say, “Here’s what I did with Harvey this month,” it carries more weight than a central team telling people what they should be doing.

kp.k: Reported power usage crosses seniority and practice boundaries
kp.d: Based on Lewis Silkin’s experience over the preceding year, Bazin reports that leading users include trainees, senior partners, lawyers in several practice areas, and non-legal teams. He characterises effective application to work—not generation or practice area—as their shared feature.
qs: Our top users span every level of the organization, from trainees through to senior partners.
It’s not generational, and it’s not limited to a specific practice area.
We see strong usage across employment, commercial, and non-legal teams.
What they have in common is that they’ve found ways to apply the technology effectively to their work.

kp.k: Lewis Silkin reports no observed generational adoption divide
kp.d: Bazin says the firm found no evidence of a generational divide during the past year, based on the consistently mixed seniority of its top users. This is a firm-specific observation; the document provides no sample size, methodology, or comparative data beyond reported usage patterns.
qs: We haven’t seen evidence of a generational divide over the past year.
If you look at our top users, it’s consistently a mix, from senior partners to junior team members.

kp.k: Seniority shapes agency while associates hold volume opportunities
kp.d: Bazin identifies two different influences on usage: senior lawyers’ confidence, autonomy, and ability to evaluate outputs enable more creative applications, while associates perform many high-volume tasks suited to Harvey, including chronologies, due diligence, and contract analysis. The source presents this as an observed interplay, without quantified task or productivity evidence.
qs: More senior lawyers tend to have greater agency — they’re confident, self-directed, and able to evaluate outputs quickly, which allows for more creative use.
At the same time, many of the most relevant use cases (chronologies, due diligence, contract analysis) sit with associates.
So there’s an interesting interplay between who can use the tool most creatively and where the highest-volume opportunities sit.

kp.k: Successful experiments should become default shared workflows
kp.d: Bazin recommends converting effective individual methods into shared best practices and making proven AI use the default approach for everyone performing the relevant task. This is a prescriptive adoption recommendation rather than evidence that all identified workflows have already been standardised.
qs: If someone has found an effective way to use the tool for a specific task, the goal is to make that the default approach for everyone doing that work.
Take the results of individual experimentation and turn them into shared best practices.

kp.k: Sustained communication and reinforcement underpin scaled adoption
kp.d: Bazin recommends a consistent communication cadence to maintain adoption momentum. In the Harvey team’s concluding synthesis, power users are described as depending on organisational systems—including clear use cases, shared workflows, and reinforcement—rather than emerging solely through isolated individual initiative.
qs: And just as importantly, you need to maintain a consistent communication cadence — that drumbeat is what keeps adoption moving.
It’s about showcasing real success stories from across the organization.
Across these conversations, one theme is clear: power users don’t emerge in isolation.
They’re supported by the right environment — clear use cases, shared workflows, and consistent reinforcement.
For organizations looking to scale adoption, the challenge isn’t just creating more power users, but building the systems that help their impact compound.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Alex Bazin describes uneven, discretionary adoption of Harvey and argues that embedding effective uses into standard workflows can turn individual experimentation into firm-wide adoption.
pts.d: Bazin reports that two-thirds of Lewis Silkin's users engage with Harvey monthly and about half of that group at least weekly. He says generative AI may improve effectiveness, profitability and client service, but individuals can still choose established working methods. His proposed response is to identify high-value uses through power users, share best practices, support practice groups through champions, and reinforce adoption through regular communications and all-hands demonstrations. Making Harvey the default for tasks such as employment-tribunal chronologies is an aspiration, not a reported firm-wide requirement. Bazin also reports that strong usage crosses seniority levels and practice areas rather than following a generational divide. He distinguishes senior lawyers' greater agency and ability to assess outputs from the high-volume opportunities in associate work. Separately, the Harvey Team's concluding synthesis claims that supportive environments and shared workflows enable power users' impact to compound.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest principally on Bazin's reported experience and usage observations at Lewis Silkin, with an additional qualitative synthesis by the Harvey Team.
pts.d: Bazin offers aggregate monthly and weekly usage proportions, observations of the firm's top users over the past year, and descriptions of implemented champions and spotlight programmes. No user count, measurement methodology or comparative adoption results are supplied. The absence of a generational divide is presented as an observation within Lewis Silkin, not a general population finding. Claims about possible profitability and client-service gains, and the effectiveness of communications and peer demonstrations, are supported by practitioner explanation rather than quantified outcome evidence. The Harvey Team attributes its broader conclusion to the conversations in its power-user series; the supplied article does not present independent testing, benchmarks or measured causal effects of the adoption programme.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview reports current adoption as of its June 2, 2026 publication, retrospective observations over the preceding year, and an ongoing aim to standardise usage without a completion deadline.
pts.d: Bazin's usage figures describe the current adoption picture; his statement about no observed generational divide explicitly concerns the past year. Driving more consistent use is his focus 'this year,' which in the publication context is 2026. Scaling and returns are prospective objectives conditioned on finding effective task-specific applications, fitting them into existing workflows, sharing practices and sustaining communications. He qualifies the potential benefits with 'may' and describes mandatory-like default usage as an ideal. Champions need workflow understanding rather than necessarily being the most advanced users. Neither Bazin nor the Harvey Team supplies a dated forecast for universal adoption or quantified future gains.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate subjects are Lewis Silkin's lawyers and non-legal staff, with different adoption opportunities for senior lawyers, associates and knowledge lawyers; clients are potential indirect beneficiaries.
pts.d: Bazin describes use from trainees to senior partners and across employment, commercial and non-legal teams. Senior lawyers are said to have the confidence, autonomy and ability to assess outputs quickly that support creative use; associates perform many relevant high-volume tasks, including chronologies, due diligence and contract analysis. Knowledge lawyers often act as champions, extending their existing training responsibilities to AI adoption. Spotlight speakers include junior marketing managers, IP disputes partners and data associates. The firm is expected to benefit through more consistent adoption, scale and potential profitability, while better client service is a possible benefit rather than a measured result. The advice is offered to other organisations seeking wider adoption, but the article makes no concrete claim about job displacement, market shares or public access to justice.
